About the editors

Dr. Utku Kose (Süleyman Demirel University, Isparta, Turkey)

Dr. Utku Kose received the BS degree in 2008 in computer education from Gazi University, Turkey, as a faculty valedictorian. He received an MS degree in 2010 from Afyon Kocatepe University, Turkey, in the field of computer science and a DS/PhD degree in 2017 from Selcuk University, Turkey, in the field of computer engineering. Between 2009 and 2011, he worked as a Research Assistant at Afyon Kocatepe University. He also worked as a Lecturer and Vocational School—Vice Director at Afyon Kocatepe University between 2011 and 2012, as a Lecturer and Research Center Director at Usak University between 2012 and 2017, and as an Assistant Professor at Süleyman Demirel University between 2017 and 2019. Currently, he is an Associate Professor at Süleyman Demirel University, Turkey. Kose also gave lectures at other higher education institutions such as Gazi University and Istanbul Arel University. He also works as a Visiting Researcher at the University of North Dakota, United States, and holds the Honorary Professor of Artificial Intelligence title at ITM (SLS) Baroda University, India. He has more than 300 publications, including articles, authored and edited books, proceedings, and reports. He is also on editorial boards of many scientific journals and serves as one of the editors of the Biomedical and Robotics Healthcare (CRC Press) and Computational Modeling Applications for Existential Risks (Elsevier) book series. His research interests include artificial intelligence, machine ethics, artificial intelligence safety, biomedical applications, optimization, chaos theory, distance education, e-learning, computer education, and computer science.

Dr. Deepak Gupta (Maharaja Agrasen Institute of Technology, Delhi, India)

Dr. Deepak Gupta is an eminent academician and plays versatile roles and responsibilities, juggling between lectures, research, publications, consultancy, community service, PhD and postdoctorate supervision, and so on. With 16 years of rich expertise in teaching and 2 years in industry, he focuses on rational and practical learning. He has contributed to massive literature in the fields of human–computer interaction, intelligent data analysis, nature-inspired computing, machine learning, and soft computing. He is working as an Assistant Professor at the Maharaja Agrasen Institute of Technology (GGSIPU), Delhi, India. He has served as an Editor-in-Chief, Guest Editor, and Associate Editor in SCI and various other reputed journals (IEEE, Elsevier, Springer, Wiley & MDPI). He has actively been organizing various reputed international conferences. He is not only backed with a strong profile, but his innovative ideas, research’s end results, and the notion of implementation of technology in the medical field are, by and large, contributing to society significantly. He completed his postdoc from the Internet of Things research group, National Institute of Telecommunications (Inatel), Brazil, in 2018; eHealth and Telemedicine Group (GTe), University of Valladolid (UVA), Spain, in 2019; Federal University of Piauí (UFPI), Teresina—Pi, Brazil in 2021; and PhD from Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam Technical University, India, in 2017. He has authored/edited 70 books with national/international-level publishers (IEEE Press, Elsevier, Springer, Wiley, CRC, DeGruyter). He has published 330 scientific research publications in reputed international journals and conferences, including 213 SCI-indexed journals of IEEE, Elsevier, Springer, and Wiley. He has also granted/published eight patents. He is the recipient of the 2021 IEEE System Council Best Paper Award and Highly Cited Paper Award in Applied Sciences journal. He has been featured in the list of the top 2% scientist/researcher database in the world in 2019, 2020, and 2022, with Rank 51 in AI & Image Processing, Rank 423 in India overall, and Rank 80,604 in the World overall. He has received a grant of Rs 1.31 CR from the Department of Science and Technology against the Indo-Russian Joint call for a project proposal on multiscale modeling of the deformation behavior of carbon fiber–reinforced high-end thermoplastics as CO-PI. He is an Associate Editor of Alexandria Engineering Journal (Elsevier), Computers and Electrical Engineering (Elsevier), Expert Systems (Wiley), Intelligent Decision Technologies (IOS Press), and Journal of Computational and Theoretical Nanoscience, Honorary Editor of ICSES Transactions on Image Processing and Pattern Recognition. He is also a Series Editor of Biomedical Engineering and Computational Modeling for Existential Risks at Academic Press, Elsevier, Intelligent Biomedical Data Analysis at De Gruyter, Germany, Explainable AI (XAI) for Engineering Applications and Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Engineering and Management at CRC Press, and Computational Intelligence for Data Analysis at Bentham Science. He has been appointed as a Consulting Editor at Elsevier. He is also associated with various professional bodies such as IEEE, ACM, ISTE, IAENG, IACSIT, SCIEI, ICSES, UACEE, Internet Society, SMEI, IAOP, and IAOIP. He has been invited as a Faculty Resource Person/Session Chair/Reviewer/TPC member in different FDP conferences and journals. He is the convener and organizer of the “DoSCI” and “ICCCNet” Springer conference series. He has also been associated with a research-based startup “ADROIDCONNECTZ.”

Dr. Jose Antonio Marmolejo-Saucedo (Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, Mexico City, Mexico)

Dr. Jose Antonio Marmolejo is a Professor at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, Mexico. His focus is on operations research, large-scale optimization techniques, computational techniques, analytical methods for planning, operations, control of electric energy and logistic systems, sustainable supply chain design, and digital twins in supply chains. He is a member of the Network for Decision Support and Intelligent Optimization of Complex and Large-Scale Systems, the Mexican Society for Operations Research, and the System Dynamics Society. He is the author of more than 30 research articles in science citation index journals, books, book chapters, conference proceedings, and presentations.

Foreword

The Earth passed through different ages and encountered many transformations since the start of everything. According to the findings, we somehow know about the Ice Age and other massive events, which changed everything radically for living organisms and ecosystems. Most of these events were actually occurrences that appeared slowly but showed high impacts at the end. Currently, we are experiencing a similar case because of the climate change. It seems that intense industrial processes and extreme use of technology are causing more carbon emissions and leading the climate change to speed up. For especially last 10 years, the effects of climate change have been worse and the change become a crisis. So, it is crucial to build effective solutions as well as prevention techniques. To do these, one way is to focus on the underlying factors and analyzing them via mathematical models.

Except from modeling systems and running tests with them, mathematical and logical background of computational methodologies also opens the doors for further analyses and accurate estimations. When we think about current research interests, these efforts can be examined under computational modeling and moved further through advanced methodologies such as data science, data analytics, and artificial intelligence. Basically, system components corresponding to the underlying factors of climate change can be carefully analyzed with computational modeling. In this way, relations among the components can be used accordingly to explain past or present cases and derive estimations for the future states. Eventually, computational modeling is among the useful tools to analyze the climate crisis and enhance ongoing research studies widely.

Considering the focus on computational modeling for climate crisis, this volume, titled Computational Modeling Applications for Climate Crisis, gathers the most recent studies and ensures a timely contribution to the literature. The chapters included in the book analyze and discuss about direct or indirect factors having effects on the climate change. I can express that especially review-based chapters enable readers to have information about essential concepts and even further topics covering the issue of climate change from different perspectives. Furthermore, the readers can read about how different areas have connections with global warming, extreme events, and broadly climate crisis and how these connections can be analyzed through mathematical definitions. I find the chapters targeting specific regions of the world remarkable since alternative outputs from such studies are helpful to figure out missing pieces of the whole puzzle of climate change. Chapters generally ensure good discussion points and expose further research ways. This book also has some chapters regarding artificial intelligence applications, which I believe have big potentials in automating the models for successful solutions. Specifically, I can suggest this book as a reference source for researchers and graduate students enrolled in engineering disciplines, mathematics, statistics, and computer science. The science of climatology would also find important findings and discussions from this book. Of course, the book will be very useful for all fields actively working on the climate crisis.

As my final words, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to Dr. Kose, Dr. Gupta, and Dr. Marmolejo Saucedo for giving me the opportunity to write a Foreword for such a timely work. I would like to also congratulate the editors and all authors for their endless efforts to end up this book. I highly suggest all readers to be lost among pages and come out with the innovative ideas in the way of further studies. With all my best wishes for the global efforts against the climate crisis.

Dr. Jafar Alzubi

Al-Balqa Applied University, Jordan

Preface

Utku Kose, Deepak Gupta and Jose Antonio Marmolejo-Saucedo

Along the long history of humankind, the planet Earth brought many challenges caused by its dynamic nature and evolving biological conditions. It is remarkable that the humankind has been always curious to understand the Earth and deal with the challenges by designing solution ways. These solution ways have been connected with especially inventions and discoveries. It is also important that the technology has been an essential component to understand the conditions deeply and advance the solution ways further. Eventually, today’s modern life seems more controllable thanks to high technology as well as more knowledge and abilities we have. However, more control over the Earth has been associated with more level of human activities which started to affect the biological conditions negatively. We currently face the threat of low natural resources, massive health problems, and extreme events caused by the climate change. Especially climate change is already an existential problem, as it showed many negative impacts within the first quarter of the 21st century.

Climate is known as a critical factor for the well-being and existence of all living organisms. It affects the well-being of generations and the sustainability of natural resources. Throughout the history, the climate has been always in a changing nature in terms of temperature levels and weather patterns. But human activities and industrial revolutions accelerated in the 20th century caused more negative changes to transform the climate change into an existential crisis. Considering especially intense use of fossil fuels and high technology, greenhouse gas emissions started to cause continuous increase in temperature values. Moreover, the climate today brings more extreme events such as storms, tornados, and heat waves. The glaciers are melting and the sea levels are rising at unexpected levels. All these situations are threat for the existence of humans, animals, and the habitat, which are all vital components of the sustainable life. So, there is a red alert for the climate crisis and there has been a worldwide intense effort to find appropriate solutions for lowering the effects of human activities as well as the high technology. Briefly, the climate crisis is an issue, which needs focus from all fields of the life. Among these efforts, there is still hope to build effective research applications, which are targeting optimized activities and use of natural resources to keep the climate change at the stable level for the next time period. At this point, it is important to inform the audience about the latest academic–scientific developments and understand more about the positive outcomes.

This book Computational Modeling Applications for Climate Crisis provides a recent collection covering modeling perspectives applied to climate change problems. The motivation of this book has been built over research perspectives, which consider mathematical aspects of climate components to derive descriptive or predictive results at the end. As the life itself is a mixture of mathematical occurrences, it is important to work with alternative computational models, which are useful for evaluating the dynamics of climate. We also believe that computational modeling should be combined with the most recent, emerging technologies so that the capabilities of solution designs can be enhanced. In this context, the book hosts a total of 12 chapters having scientific efforts by the authors around the world. In general, the book covers not only research studies but also extensive review works in the context of computational modeling and climate crisis relation. In detail, the topics include specific research problems such as precipitation forecasting, rainfall forecasting, zero carbon footprint, meteorological drought, and general weather forecasts. This book also provides views about computational modeling for agriculture and tourism. Furthermore, it is also possible to see discussions regarding responsible technology use and sustainability at the time of climate change. Because artificial intelligence reveals innovative computational solution techniques for challenging problems, some chapters are also devoted to it. These chapters include the use of traditional machine learning, quantum machine learning, deep learning, multiagent systems, and optimization-oriented approaches.

It can be seen that the active dynamics covering the life are changing rapidly, which causes the climate crisis to expand accordingly. To deal with climate crisis, one way is interpreting the parameters of systems through models, analyzing the data, and developing advanced technologies. This book accommodates the most recent advancements, which enable readers to learn about current conditions and encourage them to think about further research opportunities. We hope this reference work will be useful for the international audience and help in establishing a better future. We would like to thank all respectful authors, who made this book project a success. We also thank Dr. Jafar Alzubi for his foreword, including valuable discussions about the climate change and kind words regarding this book. Of course, we send our special thanks to all readers, who are interested in climate crisis research and alternative solutions and strategies to deal with it. Thanks for your attention. Stay aware, and responsible!

Artificial intelligence and optimized computational modelling against climate crisis

Sachin Sharma1, Ranu Tyagi1 and Seshadri Mohan2,    1Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Graphic Era Deemed to be University, Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India,    2Systems Engineering Department, University of Arkansas at Little Rock, Little Rock, AR, United States

Abstract

The climate crisis is one of the first crushing issues standing up to our planet, and addressing it requires inventive courses of action that utilize the control of advancement. Artificial intelligence (AI) and optimized computational showing have developed promising devices for dealing with this complex issue. AI can be utilized to dismember huge amount of climate data, recognize plans, and make estimates around future climate designs. By leveraging machine learning calculations, examiners can make more accurate climate models that can help policymakers make informed choices about climate action. Optimized computational illustration is another competent gadget for addressing the climate crisis. By reenacting climate systems and their intelligence, investigators can better understand the fundamental disobedient driving climate modification and make strategies for calming its influence. Together, AI and optimized computational illustration offer an able approach to understanding and responding to the climate crisis. In any case, there are vital challenges related to their utilization. These join concerns around data security, algorithmic predisposition, and the ethical suggestions of utilizing advancement to make choices that influence people’s lives. The potential benefits of AI and optimized computational display in the fight against climate change are noteworthy. By leveraging these progresses, we will choose a deeper understanding of the climate crisis and make more fruitful procedures for relieving its influence. In any case, it is imperative to carefully consider the ethical and social recommendations of their utilization and to ensure that these developments are sent in a competent and direct way.

Keywords

Artificial intelligence; optimized computational modelling; climate crisis

1.1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) might be a division of computer science that deals with making machines that can perform assignments that routinely require human experiences, such as visual acknowledgement, talk affirmation, decision-making, and dialect interpretation (Kaack et al., 2022). AI systems utilize calculations, genuine models, and computational control to analyze gigantic amounts of data, learn from plans and designs, and make estimates or choices based on that information. The climate emergency implies the complex and interconnected challenges related to climate change, counting the world temperatures, extended repeat and earnestness of uncommon climate events, rising sea levels, and the misfortune of biodiversity (Ajagekar & You, 2022). The climate crisis is caused basically by human work, particularly the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and farming. Optimized Computational Modeling may be a strategy utilized to reproduce complex systems and expect their conduct underneath unmistakable scenarios (Filho et al., 2022). It incorporates making numerical models that talk to the key components and insights inside a system and utilizing computational control to reproduce how those components modify over time in reaction to different inputs and conditions. AI and optimized computational modeling can be used as accessible tools in the fight against the climate crisis. By analyzing broad entireties of data from sensors, satellites, and other sources, AI frameworks can offer assistance to analysts and policymakers in better understanding how climate modification is impacting assorted regions and natural frameworks (Entezari et al., 2023). AI can also help recognize plans and designs in climate data that might not be immediately clear to individuals and make desires about nearly future changes inside the climate. Optimized computational modeling can help analysts and policymakers reenact the impacts of particular approach choices or mechanical intercessions on the climate. This will provide guidance on which exercises are most likely to have the most prominent influence on decreasing nursery gas surges or diminishing the impacts of climate modification (Rezaiy & Shabri, 2023). By and large, AI and optimized computational modeling are successful devices that can offer assistance to us and address the challenges of the climate crisis. By handling the control of these progresses, we will develop more compelling methods for directing the impacts of climate change and building a more viable future.

1.2 Overview of climate crisis

The climate crisis could be a complex and interconnected set of challenges related to climate change, which is the long-term move in worldwide climate designs caused basically by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and mechanical agribusiness. The resulting changes to the Earth’s climate are having broad impacts on environments, economies, and human social order. The foremost unmistakable effect of the climate crisis is the rise in worldwide temperatures, which is causing more visits and extreme heatwaves, droughts, and fierce blazes (Himeur et al., 2022). Rising temperatures are also causing the polar ice caps to melt, driving rising ocean levels that debilitate coastal communities and foundations. The climate crisis is also causing more visits and extreme climate events, such as typhoons, surges, and storms (Rane, 2023). These events can cause broad harm to property, foundations, and crops, driving financial misfortune and uprooting populations. Another major effect of the climate emergency is the loss of biodiversity, as environments are disturbed by changes in temperature and precipitation patterns. This can have far-reaching results for human social orders, as biodiversity is basic for giving biological system administrations such as fertilization, soil ripeness, and carbon sequestration (Polo-Mendoza et al., 2023). The climate crisis could be a global challenge that requires a facilitated reaction from governments, businesses, and people (Pekpostalci et al., 2023). This reaction must include a move toward more feasible solutions, such as decreasing nursery gas outflows, advancing renewable vitality, and contributing to climate adjustment measures.

1.3 Proposed methodology

AI and optimized computational roles play vital parts in addressing the climate emergency. Here are a few ways in which these innovations can be proposed and connected:

  • • Upgraded climate models: Utilize AI to move climate models forward by consolidating machine learning calculations that can analyze endless sums of climate information. This will lead to more precise expectations and recreations of future climate scenarios.
  • • Early caution frameworks: Develop AI-driven early caution frameworks for extraordinary climate phenomena, such as typhoons, surges, and dry spells. These frameworks can offer assistance to communities to get ready and react more successfully.
  • • Smart networks: Actualize AI within the administration of shrewd frameworks to optimize vitality conveyance, diminish vitality misfortunes, and coordinate renewable vitality sources more productively.
  • • Building vitality administration: Utilize AI to optimize vitality utilization in buildings through prescient analytics, keen sensors, and mechanized control frameworks.
  • • Grid integration: Utilize AI to upgrade the integration of renewable vitality sources into the control network, adjusting supply and request to guarantee a steady and dependable vitality supply.
  • • Vitality capacity optimization: Utilize AI to optimize vitality capacity frameworks, anticipate request designs, and effectively oversee vitality capacity assets.
  • • Optimized carbon capture: Apply AI to optimize the forms of carbon capture and capacity, making them more proficient and cost-effective.
  • • Monitoring and verification: Utilize AI to screen and confirm the viability of carbon capture and sequestration ventures, guaranteeing that captured carbon remains put away securely.
  • • Accuracy farming: Actualize AI in horticulture for exact cultivating, optimizing asset utilization, decreasing squandering, and minimizing natural effects.
  • • Timberland observing: Utilize AI to monitor and oversee timberlands, recognizing deforestation, surveying biodiversity, and recognizing unlawful logging.
  • • Infrastructure planning: Utilize AI to arrange and plan a framework that is versatile to the impacts of climate change, such as rising ocean levels, extraordinary climate occasions, and changing precipitation designs.
  • • Supply chain resilience: Apply AI to survey and improve the versatility of supply chains to climate-related disturbances.
  • • Situation examination: Utilize AI to analyze different climate change scenarios and their potential impacts, giving policymakers data-driven experiences for decision-making.
  • • Approach optimization: Utilize AI to optimize arrangement mediations and recognize the most compelling techniques for moderating and adjusting to climate change.
  • • Open mindfulness and engagement: Develop AI-driven instructive instruments to raise mindfulness around climate change, its causes, and potential arrangements.
  • • Community engagement: Utilize AI to encourage community engagement and collaboration in tending to nearby climate challenges.

The flowchart consists of the following steps:

  • • Information collection: Collect climate information from different sources, counting satellites, sensors, and climate-checking stations.
  • • Information preprocessing: Utilize AI calculations to preprocess and clean the collected information, dealing with lost values and exceptions.
  • • Climate modeling: Apply optimized computational models, joining AI methods to improve climate models for precision.
  • • Expectation and recreation: Utilize AI to anticipate future climate scenarios and reenact the effects of climate change.
  • • Early caution framework: Coordinated AI calculations to create an early caution framework for extraordinary climate phenomena based on the climate demonstrate expectations.
  • • Vitality productivity: Apply AI to optimizing vitality utilization and conveyance.
  • • Actualize savvy networks and build vitality administration frameworks.
  • • Renewable vitality integration: Utilize AI for effective integration of renewable vitality sources into the control network.
  • • Carbon capture and sequestration: Apply AI to optimize carbon capture forms. Created AI-driven checking frameworks for confirmation.
  • • Common asset administration: Utilized AI for exactness in horticulture to optimize asset utilization and executed AI-based woodland checking for biodiversity and unlawful action location.
  • • Climate change adjustment: Utilize AI to arrange and plan a strong foundation. Optimized supply chain flexibility utilizing AI calculations.
  • • Approach and choice back: Analyze climate change scenarios utilizing AI. Applied AI for optimizing approach intercessions.
  • • Open mindfulness and engagement: Create AI-driven instructive devices. Encouraged community engagement through the AI stage.
  • • Feedback loop: Executed criticism circles to ceaselessly make strides in models based on real-world information and changing conditions.

The proposed optimal computational model includes a computationally scalable algorithm suitable for handling complex real-world problems. The proposed algorithm is a population-based algorithm to solve problems with continuous values. The proposed algorithm can be widely applied as an optimization algorithm to solve complex problems in various engineering fields. The proposed algorithm and meta-heuristic algorithms, such as genetic algorithms, have similar operators, including crossover, mutation, and selection. However, there are some differences between them, such as that there is no preferential local search in the genetic algorithm, while the proposed algorithm supports preferential local search using different operators. In addition, the proposed algorithm is based on mutation operation, while the genetic algorithm is based on hybridization. Like other evolutionary algorithms, the proposed algorithm starts by randomly generating an initial population of 0 without a climate crisis. Then, after initialization, the search space is expanded by mutation. CCi is the mutation solution vector of EEj calculated based on Eq. (1–1):

CCi = EEj1 + Or.(EEj3 − EEj2) (1–1)

(1–1)

where Or is the optimized scaling factor varying in the range [0, 1] and determines the length of the mutation step. EEj1, EEj2, and EEj3 are solution vectors that are randomly selected, with the condition expressed by Eq. (1–2):

$\begin{array}{l} \left. {EE}_{j1},{EE}_{j2}{and}{EE}_{j3} \middle| \text{j1} \neq {j2} \neq {j3} \neq \mathit{i} \right. \\ {\mathit{i} = \left\lbrack {1, 2,\ldots\ldots.\ldots,\text{NP}} \right\rbrack} \\ \end{array}$ (1–2)

(1–2)

where i is the index of the current solution. The optimized trial climate vector (Cij) is produced by mixing the mutated vector and the parent vector in a crossover operation based on Eq. (1–3):

$\begin{array}{l} {C_{ij}{= \text{CC}}_{ij} A_{k} \leq \text{CR},} \\ {or} \\ {C_{ij}{= \text{EE}}_{ij} A_{k} > \text{CR},} \\ {k = 1,\text{2},\ldots\ldots\ldots\ldots.., n} \\ \end{array}$ (1–3)

(1–3)

where Ak is an arbitrarily chosen real number in the interval between 0 and 1. The CR is a crossover constant. If the Ak is less than or equal to CR, the optimized trial climate vector (Cij) is inherited from the mutant solution vector, otherwise, the CR is considered equal to EEij.

1.4 Advantages

The following are the advantages of artificial intelligence and optimized computational modeling against the climate crisis (Fig. 1–1):

  • • Predictive capabilities: AI and computational modeling can analyze huge sums of information from different sources and recreate complex frameworks, permitting us to form more exact expectations about future climate designs, climate occasions, and natural impacts (Pekpostalci et al., 2023).
  • • Faster processing: AI can process large amounts of information in real-time, making it conceivable to respond rapidly to changes in climate patterns and moderate the impacts of extraordinary climate occasions. This may also offer assistance in recognizing unused climate dangers and focusing on interventions to address them (Alassery et al., 2022).
  • • Improved decision making: AI and computational modeling can give decision-makers more comprehensive and exact data, making a difference in their educated choices about climate relief and adjustment measures (Polo-Mendoza et al., 2023).
  • • Identifying trends: AI can offer assistance in recognizing new trends and designs in climate information, which will be troublesome for people to distinguish. This could give modern experiences into the drivers of climate change and offer assistance in distinguishing modern arrangements to address it (Nishant et al., 2020).
  • • Optimizing resource use: Computational modeling can offer assistance to optimize asset utilization, such as renewable vitality, to maximize productivity and decrease squandering. This may offer assistance to quicken the move to a low-carbon economy (Cowls et al., 2021).
  • • Reducing costs: AI and computational modeling can offer assistance in diminishing costs related to climate research and intercessions by streamlining data collection and investigation and recognizing the most successful mediations (Rane, 2023).

1.5 Disadvantages

The following are the disadvantages of artificial intelligence and optimized computational modelling against climate crisis (Fig. 1–2):

  • • Data bias: AI models are only as great as the information they are trained on, and if the information is one-sided or incomplete, the model’s expectations can be wrong or deceiving. This could lead to inaccurate suspicions about the causes and impacts of climate change.
  • • Lack of human input: AI models can be created based exclusively on information inputs without taking into consideration the broader context and human values. This could lead to solutions that prioritize effectiveness over value or fail to consider the total range of social and natural impacts.
  • • Complexity: AI and computational models can be exceptionally complex, making it troublesome for nonexperts to get them and evaluate what comes about. This will make it difficult to communicate the findings to policymakers and the public (Rezaiy and Shabri, 2023).
  • • Technical challenges: AI and computational modeling require noteworthy specialized mastery, frameworks, and assets. This can constrain access to these instruments for smaller organizations or developing nations that will not have the assets to contribute to these advances (Bliss et al., 2021).
  • • Energy consumption: The computational control required to run AI models and simulations can consume a critical amount of energy, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions and worsening the climate crisis.
  • • Ethical concerns: AI and computational modeling can raise ethical concerns related to protection, straightforwardness, and responsibility. These concerns can be particularly critical within the context of the climate approach, where choices have far-reaching impacts on human social orders and environments (Hernández et al., 2022).

1.7 Challenges

The following are the challenges of artificial intelligence and optimized computational modeling against the climate crisis (Fig. 1–4):

  • • Information inclination: AI frameworks depend on huge sums of information to memorize and make choices, but if the information is one-sided, the AI system’s yield will also be one-sided.
  • • Need for transparency: Numerous AI frameworks are dark, making it troublesome to understand how they work, and making it challenging to recognize blunders or predispositions.
  • • Security and reliability: AI frameworks can have startling behaviors or make blunders, leading to security concerns and doubt in their reliability.
  • • Direction and morals: There are few controls overseeing the advancement and utilization of AI, and moral concerns, such as protection and segregation, must be carefully considered.
  • • Adaptability: AI frameworks can be computationally serious, making it troublesome to scale them up to handle huge datasets or complex errands.

  • • Complexity: The Earth’s climate framework is complex, with numerous forbidding factors and criticism circles, making it troublesome to precisely show.
  • • Uncertainty: Climate modeling includes numerous obscure components and suspicions, driving vulnerability within the exactness of forecasts.
  • • Resource-intensive: Computational modeling requires critical computing control, information capacity, and human assets, making it costly and troublesome to scale.
  • • Policy usage: Indeed, on the off chance that computational models precisely foresee the impacts of climate change, executing arrangements to moderate those impacts requires political will and openness.

2

Computational analysis of recurrent neural network models for precipitation forecasting: a case study in Burdur, Türkiye

Ahmet Çifci1, İsmail Kırbaş2 and Osman Tayfun Bişkin1,    1Department of Electrical-Electronics Engineering, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Burdur Mehmet Akif Ersoy University, Burdur, Turkey,    2Department of Computer Engineering, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Burdur Mehmet Akif Ersoy University, Burdur, Turkey

Abstract

Drought, a gradual and predictable disaster resulting from a decline in precipitation and water scarcity, is worsened by climate change, turning it into a local and global natural catastrophe. Addressing the impacts of reduced precipitation necessitates accurate forecasting, emphasizing the importance of anticipating droughts and efficiently managing water resources. Moreover, excessive rainfall leading to floods poses significant economic and social challenges, underscoring the need for precise precipitation predictions. Meteorological stations, satellite imagery, and weather radars are traditional tools employed in precipitation forecasting, relying on statistical methods correlating precipitation with atmospheric variables. However, these methods are computationally expensive and less practical for forecasting due to the nonlinear nature of precipitation amounts. To overcome this problem, machine learning and deep learning algorithms have become popular for precipitation prediction. Since precipitation data include both spatial and temporal information, the challenging nature of the problem requires the use of temporal information. In this chapter, we deployed recurrent models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), gated recurrent units, and long short-term memory networks for predicting the precipitation based on meteorological data from 2001 to 2018 in Burdur Province, Türkiye. The results demonstrate that RNNs and their variations are effective for predicting precipitation.

Keywords

Climate change; computational analysis; drought; precipitation forecasting; recurrent models

2.1 Introduction

Drought is a natural phenomenon that can have devastating impacts on society and the environment (Haile, Tang, Li, et al., 2020; Maleksaeidi et al., 2016; Rockström, 2003; Smucker, 2012; Wilhite et al., 2014). It occurs when there is a prolonged period of below-average precipitation, resulting in a shortage of water for human and ecological needs. Drought can lead to water shortages, land degradation, crop failure, and livestock loss, as well as social and economic disruption (Hermans & McLeman, 2021; Miyan, 2015; Nguyen et al., 2023). In recent years, the frequency and intensity of drought events have increased due to climate change, making it even more important to understand the causes of drought and develop strategies to mitigate its effects. Warmer temperatures caused by climate change are causing increased evaporation, leading to drier conditions in some areas (Haile, Tang, Hosseini-Moghari, et al., 2020). In addition, changes in land use, such as deforestation, can reduce the amount of water available for plants and animals, exacerbating the effects of drought (Chakravarty et al., 2012). It is therefore important to conserve water and protect ecosystems in order to reduce the risk of drought and its associated impacts.

Drought is a recurring and increasingly pressing environmental issue in Türkiye. Situated at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, Türkiye is blessed with a diverse climate and rich water resource potential. However, climate change, population growth, and unsustainable water management practices have made drought a serious and recurrent threat to the country’s ecosystems, agriculture, and water supply. Climate change has disrupted Türkiye’s traditional weather patterns. Rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns have led to more frequent and prolonged droughts. The country’s southern, southeastern, and central regions are particularly vulnerable (Serkendiz & Tatlı, 2023). Türkiye’s water resources are unevenly distributed geographically, with the majority of the available water resources concentrated in the country’s northeast. This makes water scarcity a significant issue in other regions, such as the Mediterranean and Aegean coasts and the eastern part of Anatolia. Agriculture is a vital sector of the Turkish economy, and it heavily relies on irrigation (Özerol et al., 2012). Droughts have had severe consequences for farmers, leading to reduced crop yields, increased production costs, and economic hardships. To address this, Türkiye has been working on improving water use efficiency and implementing drought-resistant farming practices (Yavaşlı & Erlat, 2023). Droughts also take a toll on Türkiye’s diverse ecosystems, including forests, wetlands, and rivers. Reduced water flow in rivers, for example, can disrupt aquatic habitats and harm fish populations. These environmental consequences have prompted efforts to protect and restore ecosystems affected by drought. Türkiye has been investing in water infrastructure projects, such as dams and reservoirs, to manage its water resources more effectively (Altinbilek & Hatipoglu, 2020). These projects aim to store water during wet periods for use during dry spells. However, these efforts have also raised concerns about their environmental and social impacts, including displacements and disruptions to river ecosystems. Recognizing the seriousness of the drought issue, Türkiye has developed a National Drought Management Strategy and Action Plan for 2017–23 (MoAF, 2017). This plan focuses on improving monitoring, early warning systems, and drought mitigation strategies. Cooperation with neighboring countries on water management is also crucial, as many of Türkiye’s rivers are transboundary. Public awareness and education campaigns are essential for fostering water conservation practices among the general population. Promoting responsible water usage and the importance of water-saving technologies can help reduce the impact of drought.

Burdur, a province located in southwestern Türkiye, is no stranger to the challenges posed by drought. Like many regions in Türkiye, it has faced recurring periods of water scarcity and reduced rainfall, leading to significant impacts on agriculture, ecosystems, and daily life for its residents (Reihanifar et al., 2023). Burdur Province is located in a semiarid region characterized with hot and dry summers. The province is home to several lakes, including Lake Burdur, which is a critical water source for both agricultural and domestic use. However, reduced precipitation in recent years has taken a toll on these water bodies (Davraz et al., 2019). Agriculture is a cornerstone of Burdur’s economy, with a focus on fruit orchards as well as vegetable cultivation. Drought conditions have led to decreased crop yields and increased production costs. Farmers often struggle to secure enough water for irrigation, resulting in economic hardships for the agricultural sector. Burdur relies on its lakes and reservoirs for water supply, and the prolonged droughts have depleted their water levels. This has prompted concerns about the sustainability of the region’s water supply for both agricultural and domestic purposes. Local authorities have implemented water management measures to address this issue, including water rationing during dry periods. Drought has also impacted the province’s ecosystems, including wetlands and bird habitats. Reduced water levels in lakes and rivers can disrupt the balance of local ecosystems, impacting flora and fauna. These environmental consequences highlight the need for conservation efforts and sustainable water management practices. The people of Burdur have had to adapt to changing water availability. This includes adopting more efficient irrigation methods, such as drip irrigation, and exploring drought-resistant crop varieties. Local communities also play an essential role in raising awareness about water conservation and taking measures to reduce water waste.

Predicting precipitation in Türkiye using machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models is an active area of research. Several studies have investigated the application of ML and DL models for precipitation prediction in various regions, including Türkiye. Bilgili and Sahin (2009) successfully utilized artificial neural networks (ANNs) to accurately predict long-term monthly temperatures and rainfall. The outcomes demonstrated errors that fell within acceptable limits. Saplioglu et al. (2010) developed a novel ANN prediction model to estimate daily rainfall in the meteorological stations of Burdur, Eğirdir, and Isparta in Türkiye. The study focused on improving precipitation prediction for effective water resource utilization and planning water structures. The authors compared their model with weighted average and harmonic average methods, revealing the ANN’s superior performance. Taylan and Küçükyaman (2011) also developed an effective precipitation prediction method using ANN. Their study focused on predicting precipitation in Eğirdir, located in the Lake’s Districts of Türkiye, using data from Isparta and Senirkent precipitation stations. The ANN models, with varying numbers of input variables, demonstrated improved accuracy in predicting monthly precipitation compared to historical records. The models successfully estimated missing or unmeasured data and performed well in predicting both low and high precipitation levels, highlighting the utility of the ANN approach for integrated precipitation prediction. Aydin and Çeli̇k (2013) proposed a method using satellite images and artificial intelligence (AI) to detect hazardous weather conditions in Türkiye early. They focused on predicting rainfall-related meteorological phenomena to minimize damages. Utilizing infrared satellite images, the study employed wavelet transform, principal component analysis, and classification algorithms, including ANNs and support vector machines (SVMs). The results showed an 84% prediction accuracy with ANNs and a 93% prediction accuracy with SVMs, highlighting the effectiveness of their approach. Uzelaltinbulat et al. (2019) compared the performance of different AI techniques for predicting monthly rainfall in Northern Cyprus, with the least squares SVM model showing slightly more reliable performance. Apaydin and Sattari (2020) employed a DL and geographic information system (GIS) hybrid method to model precipitation in Türkiye’s coastal zone. The study found that long short-term memory (LSTM) was the most successful method. The results also demonstrated that spatio-temporal data, coupled with the DL and GIS hybrid method, can effectively estimate precipitation and generate distribution maps in areas without direct measurements. Coban et al. (2021) developed a precipitation forecasting model for the Marmara region of Türkiye, predicting rainfall for the next 60 months (up to 2024) in its nine cities. They employed Autoregressive Moving Average, Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), and Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average models based on time series analysis, assuming past conditions persist. The ARIMA model, exhibiting the lowest estimation error, was ultimately selected as the most appropriate. Soylu Pekpostalci et al. (2023) conducted a review of studies from 2010 to 2022 on drought features in Türkiye, emphasizing types of droughts, quantifying indices, indicators, and data sources. Most studies focused on meteorological drought, with a rising trend in ML for short-term prediction. The review identified opportunities for further research in agricultural and hydrological drought monitoring, forecasting, and pattern detection in Türkiye.

While progress has been made in mitigating the impacts of the drought in Burdur, ongoing challenges remain. Sustainable water management, conservation, and long-term planning are essential to ensuring the province’s resilience to future droughts and climate variability. This chapter utilized recurrent models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), gated recurrent units (GRUs), and LSTM networks to forecast precipitation based on meteorological data recorded from 2001 to 2018 in Burdur Province, Türkiye. The aim of this chapter was to assess the effectiveness of these recurrent models in capturing the complex temporal patterns of precipitation in Burdur Province. Additionally, comparative analyses among these recurrent models were conducted to identify their strengths and weaknesses in predicting precipitation.

2.2 Methodology

2.2.1 Problem statement

In this chapter, our focus lies on utilizing DL techniques to forecast precipitation in Burdur Province. We define forecasting as the process of anticipating future values in a given time-series dataset based on its historical data points. Let x=[x1 x2…xT] denote a sequence representing time series data, where xt ∈ ℝd and d represents the number of dimensions at t. The goal of forecasting, in the context of this specific data, is to predict the values following at time T, $\left. \widetilde{\mathbf{x}} = \left\lbrack {x_{T}\quad x_{T + 1}\ldots x_{T + k}} \right. \right\rbrack$. Here k is the number of future values to be predicted. This chapter employs simple RNN, LSTM, and GRU models to forecast the precipitation in Burdur Province. Besides, we evaluate the efficacy of these models in terms of various performance metrics.

2.2.2 Recurrent neural networks

RNN models have been utilized for time series applications that demonstrate temporal dependencies (Shahid et al., 2020). They are one of the classes of neural networks that use previous outputs as current inputs in order to calculate the new output. Besides, RNN has hidden states and utilizes them with previous outputs. It allows processing input of any length, and the size of the model does not increase with the length of the input. On the other hand, RNN models have some drawbacks, such as computation time and accessing historical information. They face a challenge in accessing historical information from a long time ago because long-term temporal dependencies lead to vanishing gradient problems. The architecture of the traditional RNN unit is illustrated in Fig. 2–1.

The terms ht and ot denote the hidden state vector and output vector at the time step t, respectively. Hidden state vectors in RNN act as memory of the model and is given as follows:

ht=a1(Whhht − 1+Whxxt+ba), (2.1)

(2.1)

where a1 is the activation function and ba denotes the bias parameter. In Eq. (2.1), Whh and Whx represent the input-to-hidden and hidden-to-hidden weight matrices, respectively. The output of the RNN network can be given by

ot=a2(Wohht+bo). (2.2)

(2.2)

Here, Woh is the hidden-to-output weight matrix and bo represents the bias parameter.

2.2.3 Long short-term memory

Although RNN models can be easily applied to time series data, when dealing with long-term temporal dependencies, RNN networks face the challenge of vanishing gradient problems, which decreases their performance. To address this issue, LSTM was introduced, aiming to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Three gates—input, output, and forget gates—control the flow of information within LSTM layers (Gers et al., 2000). Input and output gates, respectively, are in charge of controlling the input and output activation information. Additionally, forget gates are employed to reset the cell memory when it is no longer necessary (Gers et al., 2000). At a specific time instance t, the input time-series data is represented as xt. Here, Wi, Wo, and Wf denote the input, output, and forget weight parameters, respectively. Consequently, the equations for the input gate (it), output gate (ot), and forget gate (ft) within the LSTM layer are as follows:

it = σ(Wi[ht − 1,xt]+bi)

ot = σ(Wo[ht − 1,xt]+bo) (2.3)

(2.3)

ft = σ(Wf[ht − 1,xt]+bf).

Here, the variables bi, bo, and bf denote the bias parameters. The vectors hf and ht represent the hidden state at time t. On the other hand, σ(.) given in Eq. (2.3) represents the sigmoid activation function. Within the LSTM layer, ht and ct are given as follows:

ct = it ⊙ c̃t + ft ⊙ ct − 1 (2.4)

(2.4)

ht = ot ⊙ tan h(ct). (2.5)

(2.5)

Here, ⊙ represents the Hadamard product and the function tan h(.) Corresponds to the hyperbolic tangent function. The expression c̃t can be given as

c̃t = tan h(Wc[ht − 1,xt]+bc), (2.6)

(2.6)

where Wc is the weight parameter and bc is the bias variable. The architecture of the LSTM unit is shown in Fig. 2–2.

2.2.4 Gated recurrent units

GRU was introduced as an alternative architecture of LSTM to simply reduce the number of parameters (Cho et al., 2014; Chung et al., 2014; Shahid et al., 2020; Zeroual et al., 2020). Unlike the LSTM model, which consists of three gates, the GRU has two gates named update and reset gates. The update gate in GRU performs a function similar to the combination of input and forget gates in LSTM, controlling the memory transferred to the new state. On the other hand, the reset gate in GRU serves a purpose akin to the forget gate in LSTM, responsible for discarding past information that is no longer relevant. The architectural diagram of the GRU unit is depicted in Fig. 2–3. The update (ut) and reset gates (rt) in GRU are given as follows:

ut = σ(Wu[ht − 1,xt]+bu) (2.7)

(2.7)

rt = σ(Wr[ht − 1,xt]+br). (2.8)

(2.8)

In Eqs. (2.7) and (2.8), Wu and Wr represent the update and reset weight parameters, respectively. Furthermore, bu and br denote the bias variables. The vector ht defined as the hidden state vector and it can be written at time step t as follows:

ht = ut ⊙ h̃t + (1−ut) ⊙ ct − 1, (2.9)

(2.9)

where h̃t is given as

h̃t = tanh (Wh[rt⊙ht − 1,xt]+bh). (2.10)

(2.10)

Here, Wh and bh are the weight parameter and bias variable, respectively.

2.3 Experiment

2.3.1 Study area and data

Burdur is a city located in southwestern Türkiye, as shown in Fig. 2–4, with a population of approximately 280,000. The city is positioned within the transition zone of the Mediterranean and Central Anatolian regions. Covering an area of around 7175 square kilometers, Burdur is characterized by diverse topography, including plains, lakes, and mountainous areas. Burdur has a warm and temperate climate with an average annual temperature of 12.2°C (Climate Data, 2023). The city has a continental climate with cold, wet, and snowy winters and hot, long, and dry summers. The average temperature in Burdur during January, the coldest month, ranges between 6.9°C and −1.1°C. August is a tropical summer month, with an average high of 32.2°C and an average low of 16.8°C (Weather Atlas, 2023). Burdur receives an average of 651 mm of precipitation annually. The wettest month is January, with an average of 88 mm of precipitation, while the driest month is August, with an average of 9 mm of precipitation (Weather & Climate, 2023). The distribution of rainfall is somewhat uneven, with a notable portion occurring during the winter months.

The dataset utilized in this chapter was sourced from the Climatic Research Unit (https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/drought/). This dataset encompasses precipitation data for Burdur Province, spanning the period from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2018. An overview of the dataset, focusing on the average monthly rainfall (in millimeters) from 2001 to 2018, is presented in Table 2–1. On the other hand, Table 2–2 provides an in-depth analysis of precipitation statistics for each individual year within the aforementioned timeframe. The tables include key metrics such as minimum, maximum, mean, median, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis values, offering a comprehensive insight into the distribution and characteristics of the precipitation data.

Fig. 2–5 depicts the graphical distributions of rainfall amounts in Burdur for each month spanning the years 2001–18. These visualizations offer insights into the dynamic nature of rainfall patterns over time, shedding light on months that have experienced notable increases or decreases in precipitation. A noteworthy trend highlighted in the figures is the diminishing rainfall in June across the years, indicative of a consistent decline in precipitation during this particular month. Additionally, the graphical representation underscores a gradual reduction in rainfall during July, pointing toward a trend of progressively drier summer months in the region. The depicted monthly variations in rainfall amounts underscore the significance of conducting thorough monthly rainfall predictions for the Burdur Province.

Based on the data presented in Fig. 2–6, it is evident that the monthly average rainfall in Burdur province exhibits a notable pattern. Specifically, the months of July and August consistently record the least amount of rainfall, implying a potential drought during the summer period. This observation suggests that the region faces a dry spell during these months over the years spanning from 2001 to 2018. Contrastingly, the figures indicate a higher precipitation rate during the spring months compared to the autumn months throughout the same time frame.

Examining Fig. 2–7, which illustrates the ratio of rainy days to nonrainy days from 2001 to 2018, it is notable that 2018 stands out as the year with the highest number of rainy days. In contrast, Fig. 2–8, which provides insight into the average rainfall amount from 2001 to 2018, indicates that there is no significant trend of decrease or increase in the average rainfall over the mentioned years. This observation suggests a relative stability in the overall amount of precipitation, implying that, on average, the region has not experienced a substantial shift in rainfall patterns during the specified time frame.

In Fig. 2–9A, the monthly average rainfall data for Burdur Province spanning the years 2001–18 is visually presented. However, it appears challenging to discern any clear trend or seasonal effects directly from the raw monthly average rainfall data. To address this limitation and gain a better understanding of the potential seasonal patterns, a seasonal decomposition analysis has been conducted and is showcased in Fig. 2–9B. The results of the seasonal decomposition, as depicted in Fig. 2–9B, offer a clearer perspective on the data.

2.3.2 Performance metrics

To assess the efficacy of simple RNN, LSTM, and GRU models, various performance metrics, including mean absolute error (MAE), mean square error (MSE), mean squared log error (MSLE), and median absolute error (MEAE), are employed. Let y be a vector representing the future values of the sequence x, defined as $\left. \mathbf{y} = \widetilde{\mathbf{x}} = \left\lbrack {x_{T}\quad x_{T + 1}\ldots x_{T + k}} \right. \right\rbrack$. Here, yi and ỹi denote actual and predicted values, respectively. The specified performance metrics are defined as follows:

${MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{n - 1}\left| {y_{i} - \widetilde{y}}_{i} \right|$ (2.11)

(2.11)

${MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{n - 1}\left( {y_{i} - \widetilde{y}}_{i} \right)^{2}$ (2.12)

(2.12)

${MSLE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{n - 1}\left( \left. {\log\left( {1 + {\widetilde{y}}_{i}} \right) - \log\left( 1 + y \right.}_{i} \right) \right)^{2}$ (2.13)

(2.13)

MEAE = median(|yi − ỹi|). (2.14)

(2.14)

Here, log(.) and median(.) represent the natural logarithm and median operator, respectively.

2.4 Results

The simulations were conducted on a PC featuring an i7-9750H CPU, 16 GB of RAM, and a processor speed of 2.6 GHz. Additionally, for accelerated model training, we leveraged the capabilities of an NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti GPU equipped with 6 GB of dedicated memory.

In forecasting the monthly average rainfall spanning from 2001 to 2018, the dataset was partitioned as follows: 80% of the complete time series data was allocated for training, 10% for validation, and the remaining 20% for testing. The test segment of the time series data was never exposed to the model during its training phase. Following the partitioning, the data underwent normalization, scaling it to a range between 0 and 1, to facilitate effective model training and evaluation.

In our experiments, model hyperparameters were established through a combination of simple search techniques. The RNN and GRU networks were configured with two layers, each encompassing 128 hidden units, supplemented by a dense layer. The LSTM model, on the other hand, featured two layers with 256 and 128 hidden units, respectively. The optimization process to minimize the loss function employed the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014), with a selected learning rate of lr=0.001. Despite setting the epoch number to 100, we implemented an early stopping method to mitigate the risk of model overfitting.

Examining the daily rainfall data, it becomes apparent that the signal is characterized by a high level of noise. Therefore we determined that for more effective and suitable predictions, utilizing moving averages (MA) of the time series data over longer intervals would be beneficial. To this end, we conducted experiments and predictions employing three distinct approaches: the 3-month MA, the 6-month MA, and the 12-month MA.

Figs. 2–10 to 2–12 depict the simulation results of rainfall amounts obtained through the utilization of 3-month MA, 6-month MA, and 12-month MA, respectively. The training, validation, and test splits can be seen in the figures. Notably, the most favorable outcomes are observed when employing the 12-month MA, attributed to a significant reduction in noise compared to the 3-month MA and 6-month MA.

Table 2–3 provides a comprehensive overview of model performances, measured in terms of MAE, MSE, MSLE, and MEAE metrics. The metrics showing the most successful model performance values for the 3-, 6- and 12-month MA are marked in bold. While the LSTM model exhibits commendable performance with the 6-month MA, the GRU model surpasses other models in the 3- and 12-month MA scenarios. Conversely, the performance of the simple RNN lags behind when compared to the other models.

2.5 Conclusion

This chapter focused on predicting precipitation levels in Burdur Province. The daily and monthly precipitation data exhibit significant noise, prompting our approach to utilize 3-, 6-, and 12-month MA for predictions. GRU, LSTM, and traditional RNN models were deployed for this purpose. The predictive performances of these models were assessed using metrics such as MAE, MSE, MSLE, and MEAE. Upon comparing the models, the GRU model emerges as the superior performer, particularly for the 3- and 12-month MA of precipitation, outpacing other models across these metrics. On the other hand, for 6-month MA, GRU excels in terms of MSLE, while the LSTM model demonstrates superior performance in terms of MAE, MSE, and MEAE metrics when compared to other models.

Due to the high frequency of nonrainy days throughout the year, the dataset contains a significant number of zero values. Moreover, the precipitation amount does not demonstrate a consistent upward or downward trend over the year; instead, it adheres to a distinct seasonal pattern. Therefore predicting on a daily basis proved to be less successful, and forecasting on a seasonal basis yielded more accurate results.

Sustainable development goal-13: a case of zero carbon footprint

Prisilla Jayanthi Gandam,    CMR Institute of Technology, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Abstract

Sustainable development goals are initiated in all countries to promote a healthy atmosphere and reduce carbon dioxide emissions worldwide. The aim is not just for any individual state or person; rather, it is a national concern. The zero carbon footprint involves cooperation from various sectors that include industries, hospitals, residential buildings, and transportation. In this study, the emphasis is on the carbon emissions impacting climate change, which in turn distracts the whole ecosystem. However, the overall SDG index score of India is 54, and CO in Anand Vihar reached 120 ppm in February–March 2020. The geospatial techniques of were implemented for climate change adaptation and mitigation. The key is to save energy and reduce carbon emissions by using clean and green electricity.

Keywords

Carbon; climate change; ecosystem; electromagnetic field; radiation; renewable energy; solar power

3.1 Introduction

The Sustainable Development Goal framework is to provide social, environmental, and economic progress. In the SDG, Goal-13 deals with climate action that relates to carbon emissions. It requires waste elimination in production and an increase in yield savings.

This pandemic year affected many lives and livelihoods, leading to the climate crisis and impacting global economic loss and social life. It was an unknown and unexpected pandemic that affected human lives. Though the decline of CO2 emissions significantly fell by 6.4% in the transportation sector, a huge increase was found in the healthcare industry with all the waste disposals. The emergency decision to reduce carbon emissions by half by 2030 and reach net-zero carbon by the year 2050 with 1.5°C was stated globally. A remarkable statement at the Paris Agreement and the adoption of the SDG go hand-in-hand.

Science clearly states that if one sector fails to meet these goals, society’s economy is disrupted. SDGs and targets are integrated and applied universally, considering different national realities, capacities, and development levels and saluting national policies and priorities. The global level of ambition is that the energy sector achieves the goal. The production and use of energy are the major sources of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In the atmosphere, CO2 levels and other GHG made new records in 2019; the year happens to be the second warmest year. Coal is the leading emitter of GHG, and coal is the enemy of the human race, polluting the environment globally.

In the year 2020, with the COVID-19 pandemic, a major drop of 6% in GHG emissions was found due to travel bans and economic stoppages. Transport emissions account for around 60% of oil demand, and the drop in oil demand contributed the largest share to the decline in 2020 emissions (IEA, 2021 https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/charts/change-in-co2-emissions-by-fuel-1990-2020). A large portion of the energy use in the transport zone is fueled by oil, which releases toxic air pollutants and GHGs (Guttikunda & Jawahar, 2012). One of the largest polluting industries is healthcare, responsible for nearly 5% of the total global GHG (Sherman, 2021; Jayanthi & Muralikrishna, 2023). The use of electric vehicles will eliminate CO2 emissions by 2030 and establish automated smoke detectors/sensors for vehicles on smart roads connecting major cities. The COVID-19 did not pause climate change (CC), but when the pandemic disappears, emissions are expected to return to extreme levels (https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/climate-change/).

Yet another reason for India’s pollution problem is unhealthy levels of ambient PM2.5, and setting a goal to achieve a new zero-carbon target is a challenge. The assurance of ensuring minimal emissions will require transforming the significant sectors of the economy—energy, transport, agriculture, industry, and buildings. This transformation aims to produce less waste, use resources more efficiently, and promote sustainable production and consumption. This revolution is a challenge for the pollution problems of persistent air and water. In the last year, emissions grew throughout the entire world.

3.2 Discussion and results

The state-of-the-art climate model signifies a gradual increase in torrential rain events with an upcoming warmer world. This event clearly proves how societies are not resilient to current weather extremes. One needs to reduce GHG emissions as early as possible, thereby creating and refining emergency alerts among the people and management systems and making the infrastructure “climate resilient”—to lessen the casualties and costs and make them withstand these disasters of extreme sudden flooding (Nijhuis, 2021). Global warming is the major cause of indefinite rainfalls.

3.2.1 Sea level increase

In a discussion, a scientist from the IPCC stated that the global sea level will rise from 0.3 to 1 m by the year 2100. Simultaneously, the sea level is rising around 2.3 m with every degree the planet is warmed. The question of how long it takes for the sea level to rise with the increase in temperature still remains unknown to researchers (Willis et al., 2018). According to the survey, the largest temperature rise was in the years 1910–45 and later in 1975. However, if no preventive measures were considered to reduce CO2 emissions and other GHGs. By 2100, temperatures would rise by 5°C and predicted sea levels would rise by 48 cm because of globalized human wealth (Enzler, 2021).

3.2.2 Radiation from cell phones or towers

Researchers from Kolkata’s Jadavpur University have experimented by exposing nearly 50 mirch plants to mobile radiation from the seed stage. Professor Bhaskar stated that in the comparison with nonexposure to radiation (normal plants) with these plants, the exposure leaves were found to be wrinkled and looked dull. It proved that plants are affected by mobile radiation (Cell phone radiation affects plants, vegetables: Research, 2016). In another study, researchers from the Salim Ali Centre for Ornithology and Natural History, Coimbatore, and studies in Spain and Belgium claim that bird mortality is caused by electromagnetic radiation (EMR). According to Punjab University, EMR damages bird eggs and embryos (Ram, 2008). The study reveals that the emission of radiation from cell phone towers and mobile phone handsets is causing side effects on honey bees (Santhosh, 2018). High-level damage to trees is observed within the neighborhood of mobile towers. The demonstration using the statistical analysis of EMR from mobile phone towers was harmful to trees. The results were reliable with the trees damaged by mobile phone towers, which started on one side gradually and extended to the whole tree over time (Waldmann-Selsam, 2016). The researcher suggests that there is an increase in indoor concentrations of air pollutants due to the use of certain types of chemicals in home products, inadequate ventilation, and electronic smog radiation. This concludes that radiation gradually decreases the number of trees and birds. As the trees are affected, the surrounding area is more susceptible to carbon dioxide pollutants and other pollutants released the transport. In this way, indirectly, EMF radiation causes global warming in society.

3.2.3 Emission from information communication and technology industries

ICT industries revolutionized the economic growth of the state/country with the various industries they developed. The researchers and analysts estimated that at most 50 billion devices will be added to ICT by 2020; statistical outcomes prove more than 100 billion upcoming five years down the line. The data centers, the largest energy consumers on the planet, have a large share of GHG emissions, beating the energy consumption levels of many countries (Reports on the Increasing Energy Consumption of Wireless Systems and Digital Ecosystem, 2021). A tremendous amount of energy is consumed in developing any AI system. Moreover, ChatGPT emits CO2 (8.4 tons) per year; by promoting sustainable practices in AI R&D (Sophie, 2023), one can reduce the emissions.

From McMaster University (Canada), the researchers stated that GHG from ICT, which includes computers, phones, and data centers, would increase global emissions from 1% (2007) to over 14% (2040). The existing carbon footprint of the global transportation sector was reduced by half (Garg et al., 2011). The overall contribution of CO2 emissions from the ICT industries has a huge impact on CC. In an EU report, researchers estimated that to keep the global temperature rise below 2°C, a decrease in carbon emissions of around 15%–30% is essential by the year 2020 (Patel, 2018). However, due to the pandemic, the carbon emissions from PCs did not reduce but increased. Most of the work and shopping (essentials and groceries) were carried out online during the lockdown. 1 kWh of electricity is required to download 300HD movies in 4G; however, with 5G, one kWh can download 5K UHD movies (Cho, 2020).

3.2.4 Artificial neural network—calculation for emission rate

The ANN model (Fig. 3–1) is implemented for the computation of Greenhouse gas emissions calculations (n.d.) (https://www.pca.state.mn.us/business-with-us/), to produce more accurate results for analyzing carbon net zero. This model trains the different pollutants that are taken as inputs to predict the carbon concentration. All these parameters are multiplied by the weights and passed into the various hidden layers to produce the results. This prediction will help to minimize the number of pollutants in any particular location or region. The calculation of the emission rate is shown in Fig. 3–1. This study involves air quality index data from the city of Anand Vihar, Delhi, from February 26 to March 27, 2020. Fig. 3–2 depicts the amount of CO and other pollutants, mainly PM2.5, PM10, and NO2 emissions in Delhi. Fig. 3–3 shows the levels of the Air Quality Index from February 26 to March 27, 2020.

3.2.5 Pollutant emission and air quality index—Delhi 2020

Fig. 3–2 represents different pollutants, namely CO, PM2.5, PM10, SO2, NO2, Ozone, and NH3, from February 26 to March 27, 2020. PM10 was at its maximum on March 2, 2020, with poor air quality in the atmosphere.

Fig. 3–3 represents the readings of AQI in Anand Vihar and was found to have a low value of 71 among the data collected on March 27, 2020. Carbon monoxide is low on March 13, 2020 (Fig. 3–4). Carbon monoxide is emitted by cooking gas, natural gas, wood, motor vehicles, power plants, wildfires, and incinerators. CO-poisoning correlates with human blood directly (Rose et al., 2017). PM2.5 (Fig. 3–5) is high on March 2 (284) and minimum on March 27 (49).

Fig. 3–6 indicates AQI versus CO emission. Similarly, Fig. 3–7 represents PM10 versus PM2.5, which is emitted from construction sites, fires, unpaved roads, and smokestacks. PM particles, when inhaled by humans, get deep into the lungs. enter the bloodstream. and poses a risk to the chronic respiratory system.

3.2.6 Renewable energy, clean energy, and hydropower

The purpose of SDG Goal-13 (climate action) is to increase the percentage of renewable energy out of the total installed generating capacity by November 2020. The global target is to integrate CC measures into national policies, planning, and strategies in all 37 states.

It aims to take urgent action to cope with CC and its impact. The whole world is experiencing sea level rise, an increase in GHG concentrations that is harmful to lives. With rising GHG emissions, ambitious plans and actions are needed for CC adaptation and mitigation (Sustainable Development Goals: National Indicator Framework, 2020).

Table 3–1 shows that India needs to contribute a lot to minimizing CO2 emissions to improve its score above 70%. As of now, the overall performance of India is only 54%; cooperation from severity states is very essential in improving overall performance.
