8.6.1 Hourly trends of air pollutants in Visakhapatnam

The hourly data for Visakhapatnam and Shastri Nagar was collected for six consecutive days in April, July, December 2022, and January 2023. The trends clearly show low pollution during the rainy season (Jayanthi & Muralikrishna, 2022). The x-axis and y-axis represent the number of hours and the pollutant quantity, respectively.

In the data collected to measure the air quality index (AQI), there are multiple independent variables (monthly graphs) such as PM2.5, PM10, CO, NO2, and a dependent variable (AQI); hence, it is called a multivariate time series. In multivariate time series, trend graphs have more than one time series variable. Each variable does not depend on its historical data but depends on other variables.

The equation is given by:

 Z1(t) = a1 + w110 * y1(t−1) + w111 * y2(t−1) + e1(t−1) (8.3)

(8.3)

 Z2(t) = a2 + w120 * y1(t−1) + w121 * y2(t−1) + e1(t−1) (8.4)

(8.4)

here,

  • a1 and a2 are the constant terms,
  • w10, w11, w20, and w21 are the coefficients,
  • e1 and e2 are the error terms

Similarly, for univariate trend graphs (hourly graphs), single dependent and independent variables, the linear regression equation is given as:

a = mb + c (8.5)

(8.5)

here,

  • a=independent variable
  • b=dependent variable
  • m=slope
  • c=y-intercept
  1. A. April month
    For Visakhapatnam, in April (Fig. 8–2A), the observation was made from April 25 to 30, 2022. On April 27, PM2.5 was the minimum with a range of 39–42; similarly, CO was the minimum with a range of 20–34 on April 29; NO2 was the minimum with a range of 38–43 on April 30; and PM10 was 95–106 on April 28.
  2. B. July month 2022
    In July (Fig. 8–2B), the readings were considered from July 20 to 25, 2022. On July 24, both PM2.5 (40–46) and NO2 (39–40) were found to have the minimum range; similarly, on July 25, both CO (11–23) and PM10 (79–87) were found to be minimum.
  3. C. December month 2022
    In December 2022 (Fig. 8–2C), the observation was gathered from December 1 to 6, 2022. On December 2, both PM2.5 (114–119) and PM10 (110–113) had minimum values. Similarly, on December 4, the minimum range of CO (16–45) and NO2 (30–35) was noted.
  4. D. January month 2023
    The observations considered in this month were from January 1 to 6, 2023 (Fig. 8–2D). On January 3, PM2.5 was minimum within the range of 73–93; similarly, CO was minimum within the range of 19–31 on January 1. On January 2, both NO2 (28–33) and PM10 (86–110) were at their minimum.

8.6.2 Air quality index hourly trends: April, July, December 2022, and January 2023—Visakhapatnam

The trends of AQI show the increase and decrease of the quality of air in the atmosphere in Visakhapatnam (Fig. 8–3) for April, July, December, and January. On July 25, the minimum AQI was 79–87 and the highest AQI was 308–314 on December 6, 2022, based on the reading considered for this study.

8.6.3 Monthly trends of air pollutants in Visakhapatnam for April, July, and December 2022

The monthly trends (Fig. 8–4) represent minimum CO (July), NO2 (July), PM2.5 (April), and PM10 (July), and the highest PM2.5 in December. The analysis proves that during the rainy season, that is, July (Fig. 8–3), the pollutants are found to be minimal with better air quality. The rain washes the pollutants from the atmosphere, keeping the atmosphere clean and with fresh air quality. Rain helps to increase the air quality (Fig. 8–15). This process is known as wet deposition.

8.6.4 Monthly trends of air quality index in Visakhapatnam

Fig. 8–5 represents the monthly trends with dates on the x-axis and AQI on the y-axis for the three corresponding seasons. It is clearly evident that AQI ranges from 40 to 119 for July, April and May ranges between 34 and 151, and in November and December, AQI ranges from 73 to 294.

8.6.5 Hourly trends of air pollutants in Shastri Nagar

In hourly trends, one can observe that PM10, PM2.5, and CO have high values in the dry summer, that is, April, whereas in December and January (winter), CO and NO2 have minimum values (Fig. 8–6C and D). July has better AQI values (Fig. 8–7).

  1. A. April month 2022
    In April (Fig. 8–6A), Shastri Nagar had a minimum CO (22–35) on April 26. Similarly, on April 29, both PM2.5 (103–114) and PM10 (123–127) were found to be minimums, and NO2 (115–119) on April 28.
  2. B. July month 2022
    In July (Fig. 8–6B), the minimum CO (31–40) was observed on July 21. Similarly, on July 22, PM2.5 (36–41) and PM10 (42–49) on July 25 were minimums, and NO2 (40–41) on July 23 and 24.
  3. C. December month 2022
    In December (Fig. 8–6C), Shastri Nagar had a minimum PM10 (152–162) on December 4. Similarly, on December 6, both PM2.5 (127–134) and CO (20–53) were found to be at their minimum, and NO2 (39–48) on December 1.
  4. D. January month 2023
    In January (Fig. 8–6D), Shastri Nagar had a minimum CO (17–26) on January 1. Similarly, on January 2, both PM2.5 (91–109) and PM10 (111–129) were found to be at their minimum, and NO2 (42–49) on January 3.

8.6.6 Air quality index hourly trends: April, July, December 2022 and January 2023—Shastri Nagar

The trends of hourly AQI (Fig. 8–7) were minimal on April 29 (124–129), July 22 (41–47), December 4 (152–162), and January 2 (111–130). This clearly proves that the rains wash away the pollutants in the air, thereby improving the air quality. In winter, the air quality is very poor.

8.6.7 Monthly Trends of Air Pollutants in Shastri Nagar in April, July, and December 2022

The trends of pollutants (Fig. 8–8) show PM2.5 (330) and PM10 (368) are found to peak on May 22, CO (79) on November 11, and NO2 (205) on December 2, 2022. Similarly, AQI (Fig. 8–9) has a maximum (368) on May 22 and a minimum (42) on July 26.

8.6.8 Monthly trends of air quality index in Shastri Nagar

An AQI value (Fig. 8–15) indicates the quality of the air in the atmosphere. It ranges from April (111–261), May (144–368), July (42–74), November (102–261) and December (71–212).

8.6.9 Hourly trends of air pollutants in Nehru Nagar (Delhi)

In hourly trends, one can observe PM10, PM2.5, and CO have high values in winter months, that is, December 2022 and January 2023, whereas in July (rainy), CO and NO2 have minimum values (Fig. 8–10) with better AQI values (Fig. 8–12).

  1. A. April 2022
    For the month of April, the readings were considered from April 1 to 6, 2022 (Fig. 8–10A). Nehru Nagar had a minimum CO (59–68) on April 5. Similarly, on April 3, both PM2.5 (228–251), NO2 (104–119), and PM10 (184–262) were found to be at their maximum on April 1.
  2. B. July 2022
    In July month (Fig. 8–10B), the readings were considered for July 8–14, with minimum CO (18–24) on July 8 and PM2.5 (43–50) on July 14, and on July 12, maximum PM2.5 (125–174) was observed. Both PM10 (63–79) and NO2 (35–41) were at their minimum on July 10.
  3. C. December 2022
    For the study of winter, the readings were collected from December 25 to 31 (Fig. 8–10C). Minimum CO (17–34) was found on December 31, NO2 (84–104) was maximum on December 29, and both PM2.5 (413–437) and PM10 (340–359) were maximum on December 30.
  4. D. January 2023
    In January (Fig. 8–10D), Nehru Nagar had a minimum CO (22–41) on January 3. Similarly, on January 6, PM2.5 (414–462), PM10 (348–445), and NO2 (81–94) were found to be maximum.

8.6.10 Monthly trends of air pollutants in Nehru Nagar (Delhi) in April, July, and December 2022

The air pollution trends (Fig. 8–11) show PM2.5 (480) and PM10 (435) are found to peak on November 4, CO (152) on May 9, and NO2 (128) on May 6, 2022. Similarly, AQI (Fig. 8–12) has a maximum (480) on November 4 and a minimum (38) on July 30.

8.6.11 Air quality index hourly trends: April, July, December 2022, and January 2023—Nehru Nagar

From the trends of hourly data, AQI (Fig. 8–12) was lowest on April 5 (204–248), July 10 (63–79), December 28 (344–373), and January 1 (320–351). This clearly proves that the rains wash away the pollutants in the air, thereby improving the air quality. In winter, the air quality is very poor.

8.6.12 Monthly trends of air quality index in Nehru Nagar

An AQI value (Fig. 8–13) indicates the quality of the air in the atmosphere. It ranges from April (201–337), May (116–321), July (38–190), November (256–480), and December (191–455).

8.7 The need for an air quality index

AQI helps people know how the local air quality impacts one’s health. In the USA, every year, it is estimated that bad-quality air is responsible for 100,000 premature deaths. In India, the estimated deaths are calculated at 670,000 deaths annually. Whenever one breathes air pollutants, they enter the bloodstream and contribute to coughing and itchy eyes, worsening many breathing problems that can lead to cancer and premature deaths as well. Air pollution causes diseases related to the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. Hence, AQI helps to assess and compare short- and long-term diseases at any location. Pollutants like smoke or haze can reduce visibility in the atmosphere. AQI values around or below 100 are generally good or satisfactory (Table 8–9). Table 8–9 represents the comparative values of PM2.5 and corresponding AQI on April 15 for the years 2019, 2020, 2022, and 2023 for three different states: AP (Visakhapatnam), RJ (Shastri Nagar), and Delhi (Nehru Nagar). From the readings, one can observe that PM2.5 and AQI are increasing in NN, whereas SN had the highest in 2021, but for Visakhapatnam, there was a drastic rise in AQI and PM 2.5 values. The graph (Fig. 8–14) represents the variation of the values.

The winter season increases the pollution in the air with the use of more personal vehicles. Moreover, the use of firewood and fireplaces to keep the rooms’ inside/outside warm leads to an increase in pollution. In winter, the air pollution remains in the atmosphere for much longer and is breathed at a higher rate than during the summer. As in the rainy season (Fig. 8–15), air quality is good. The choropleth state maps in Fig. 8–15 are produced by QGIS software. Due to a lack of data from Delhi state rainfall, the authors would not map. Here, one can see at a glance that the rainfall was high in 2009 and decreased in the upcoming years (2019 and 2022). The cause is the increased pollution in the atmosphere, thereby increasing global warming. Also, one can observe good air quality in snowy places. Snow reduces the pollutants in the air by absorbing pollutants into it and improving the quality of the air in the atmosphere.

8.8 Waste to energy—recycle of PM2.5

The waste industries today are in every corner and in every heart of the circular economy. Industry 4.0 involves different technologies working toward waste management that have different phases: waste generation, storage, collection, waste disposal, and waste treatment (ISWA [2021–2030], n.d.). However, industry 5.0 involves 6R: recognize, reconsider, realize, reduce, reuse, and recycle, and the principle of logistics efficiency design. The four R’s—repair, reduce, reuse, and recycle—are essential to thinking about zero waste. Recycling is one of the significant outcomes of industrial upcycling, which involves process waste; empty moving transport vehicles on the roads come under process waste (Demir & Cicibaş, 2019).

Industry 5.0 aims to be human-centric with the development of assistive technology and provide a move toward environmental goals (Turner et al., 2022). CC has negative impacts on waste generation. However, waste treatment and disposal may have both positive and negative climate impacts. Hence, increasing activities of waste management reduce GHG emissions (Waste and Climate Change: Global trends and strategy framework. United Nations Environmental Programme Division of Technology, n.d.). Waste is not an issue but is a part of the solution and is a significant source of renewable energy; the energy value can be utilized through thermal processes such as incineration and industrial co-combustion. Waste hierarchy (Waste and Climate Change: Global trends and strategy framework. United Nations Environmental Programme Division of Technology, n.d.) includes waste prevention, reuse, recycling, waste to energy, and land fill, where energy waste occurs (Fig. 8–16). PM2.5 recycling is discussed in this study.

Disposal of e-waste and recycling activities emits PM (Bungadaeng et al., 2019) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) (Gu et al., 2010), which are exposed to workers and nearby residents, causing various diseases. According to the study by Zheng et al. (2016), PM2.5 consists of carcinogenic and noncarcinogenic elements and PAH that are at higher risk for human health, especially children than adults. Recycling of e-waste, emission controls, and protective measures for workers are not available or informed at an early stage (Kwarteng et al., 2022).

ANDRITZ fabric filters are used to collect PM emissions, ash recirculation, and the absorption of partially gaseous pollutants. A wet electrostatic precipitator is used to accumulate submicron particulate and aerosols (PM10) from gas streams (Clean air for better tomorrow. Air Pollution Control, n.d.).

In heavy diesel vehicles, diesel particulate filters are used, but no particulate filter is found in most fuel vehicles or light-duty automobiles due to their expensive cost. Han et al. (2015) have proposed a self-powered triboelectric filter for eliminating PMs from vehicle exhaust fumes with the effect of triboelectrification. The triboelectric filter has a very huge collection capacity with an efficiency of PM2.5 (~95.5%) using the self-vibration of the tailpipe.

8.8.1 Waste to value energy conversion: PM2.5 for electrodes

From a diesel vehicle, with an air metric MV portable sampler attached to the engine exhaust, PM2.5 samples were produced and gathered. During the observation study, for every hour of collection, PM2.5 (4–5 mg) samples were gathered (Fig. 8–17) from filter membranes (PTFE) in an air sampler. Then, later at 900°C, annealing PM2.5 samples for one hour under the flow of an Ar (100sccm), and sequentially cleaned with 5 wt.% HF, HCl (1.0M), deionized water, ethanol, and finally at 110°C, dried throughout the night. After annealing and purification, the left-out elements are mostly carbon and a minor quantity of O2 and N (doping elements). XPS analyses the chemical states and atomic ratios of N, O, and C elements present in the PM − CNPs. Supercapacitors, with an outstanding storage capacity of charging with a specific capacitance $\left( 134.4\frac{F}{g}{in} 6.0M{KOH} \right)$ at a current density $\left( 0.1\ \frac{A}{g} \right)$ and good stability over 5000 cycles found in  PM − CNP. PM − CNPs have a unique structure and composition, which are excellent electrode materials for supercapacitors. Finally, the overall outcomes proved the development of an effective strategy for the recycling of high-performance carbon material from PM2.5 aerosols. Hence, the PM − CNPs offer an innovative electrode material with greater possibility in energy conversion and storage, combined with higher penetrability, electrochemical activity, and stability (Zhu et al., 2017).

8.9 Nanotechnology toward waste to energy

The sustainability of the environment is concerned with global CC and pollution, be it water, soil, or air. In this chapter, the study focuses on the air pollutant, that is, PM2.5, and its impact on human health (Sun, 2019). Let us discuss more in detail how environmental contamination can be resolved using a technology-based solution. One such solution is the innovative nanotechnology that provides the ability to detect, perceive, and treat the contamination concentration in the air. The largest contamination confronted by the world is environmental contamination with organic and inorganic compounds. Air, water, and soil are mainly affected by lots of dangerous waste from the revolution of industrialization. Nanomaterials are outstanding adsorbents, catalysts, and sensors. Also, the nanomaterials have unique properties—physicochemical, superficial, and optical electronic—that resolve difficult issues that cannot be treated with conventional technologies. Environmental pollution is harmful to humans when one inhales, ingests, or absorbs it (Mohamed, 2017).

8.9.1 Nanotechnology in plastic recycle

The low cost and durability of plastic have occupied the main place in humans’ lives, be it everyday household products, industrial packing material, hospitals, and so on. Plastics do not undergo biodegradation but rather form microplastics that enter oceans, causing water pollution and indirectly air and environmental pollution. The water smells foul and spreads into the air, polluting the nearby residential areas. These microplastics are found in drinking water, cooking salt, and other food products (enter the live fish) that cause harm to human life. Nanoadditive use improves mechanical and optical properties of recycled materials and nanocatalyst development for plastic depolymerization. Nanoparticles act as catalysts for plastic depolymerization.

The nanoadditives are of two types: organic and inorganic materials. Organic material consist of carbon-derived components such as graphene, carbon nanotubes (CNT), and nanocellulose. However, in inorganic nanoadditives, metal oxide materials, that is, ZnO, TiO2, and SiO2 nanoparticles, are present in the recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) and polypropylene as inorganic nanoreinforcements to improve the mechanical properties (Distaso, 2020). Hence, these nanoparticles help the recycling of plastic to be used in a better way and save environmental pollution by reducing GHG and, overall, saving energy. Here, the waste is reused to save energy.

8.9.2 Nanotechnology: a unique solution for air pollution

The unique reactive properties, that is, adsorbents, catalysts, and sensors of nanoparticles, play a promising approach to overcoming air pollution abatement (Kumar et al., 2022).

8.9.2.1 Catalyst

Nanostructured catalyst material has a special property for air pollution control applications. Nanospheres, nanoplates, nanotubes, and nanoaerogels are present in this catalyst material; it has inherent performance and excels in physiochemical stability (Nasrollahzadeh et al., 2020). Certain catalysts remove volatile organic compounds from industrial smoke outlets, which pollute the environment. The catalyst is known as a nanofiber catalyst, produced from manganese oxide. Researchers from the University of Queensland experimented with a nanomaterial named CNT used for collecting GHG emissions caused by mining coal and power generation. This CNT traps gases 100 times faster than other techniques. Further, a magnetic nanocatalyst ((CH3)3−NHC−Pd@Fe3O4) is an outstanding catalyst for decreasing toxic environmental pollutants. At room temperature, Manjunatha et al. (2021) suggested the magnetic nanocatalyst reduces the toxic 4-nitrophenol, hexavalent chromium, methylene blue, and methyl orange in a water-based solution. The purpose of nanocatalysts with an increased surface area is to speed up chemical reactions that convert harmful waste vapors from cars and industrial plants to useful gas (Turning to Nanotechnology for Pollution Control: Applications of Nanoparticles, 2009) (https://sites.dartmouth.edu/). Moreover, by storing the oxygen, nanocatalysts support complete fuel combustion, thereby reducing the emission of GHG (Chausali et al., 2023).

8.9.2.2 Nanosensors

The efficiency of nanosensors in detecting toxic gases such as NO2, sulfur dioxide, and hydrogen sulfide is appreciable (Manjunatha et al., 2021).

8.9.2.3 Nanobioremediation

Nanosized particles have a large surface area, thus improving chemical and biological reactivity. Nanobioremediation reduces the environmental contamination concentration to low levels. Nanotech processes and applications contribute to the environment with elimination protection by saving raw materials, energy, and water and reducing GHG and hazardous wastes (Haleema et al., 2022).

8.10 Photoelectrochemical: carbon dioxide

Photoelectrochemical (PEC) CO2 conversion is an artificial photosynthesis approach and the best approach to converting CO2 into selective gaseous and liquid products under solar light irradiation. During PEC CO2 conversion, the endothermic reactions are determined by electricity and light irradiation. Similarly, the photogenerated electrons’ energy levels and holes have to be higher than the overpotential of H2O/O2 and lower than the overpotential of CO2/HCOOH for feasible CO2 conversion. The outcome of CO2 conversion is selected by the choices of the materials involved in electrodes and electrolytes (Kumaravel et al., 2020).

8.11 Conclusion

The air pollution and AQI were studied in three states, AP, Delhi, and RJ. The GLM regression model was applied to the dataset. It was observed that the z-score values of PM2.5 and PM10 were high in the winter over the rainy season due to various factors of emissions. Air quality was much better in these states during the rainy season. PM2.5 emissions are an increased risk for the human respiratory system, causing cancer. However, waste-to-energy technologies proved air pollutants, such as PM2.5, that are highly human-risk can be converted to useful energy. Captured PM2.5 can be used for electrodes in supercapacitors.

Chapter 9

Development of deep learning models for climate change within python framework

Hemaraju Pollayi1, Praveena Rao2, Dathathreya Chakali1 and Pratyusha Bandaru1,    1Department of Civil Engineering, GITAM University, Hyderabad, Telangana, India,    2Department of Civil Engineering, Institute of Aeronautical Engineering, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

Abstract

Climate crisis is the risk posed by global warming to planet and humanity, and therefore it is essential to develop deep learning (DL) models for mitigating climate change. Even the most advanced computers are unable to accurately replicate the planet’s climate due to its complexity. The rise in global temperature, a long-term warming of the planet, is owing to the emissions from flaming fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas. The global and regional climatic models are developed based on the recurrent neural networks (RNNs) considering the real-life data which includes topography, land cover, and soil types These global models are helpful for comprehending how human behavior affects the entire planet. The geographical models, usually a few tens of kilometers, are zooming in on specific areas with finer resolutions and better suited to study the effects on agriculture, diseases, and specific ecosystems. The operations performed in python framework are loading a raw dirty dataset, cleaning, and preprocessing. The dataset is fed into the models for exploring the visualizations regionally and globally. The global temperature trend is predicted after training the models and evaluating the performance of these models. Popular neural networks such as RNN, long short-term memory, and gated recurrent unit are implemented using various optimizers like Adam, SGD, Adamax, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSProp, and Nadam for predicting the global temperature trend and assessing the performance of the models. Finally, the DL models illustrated in the present work could be utilized to forecast the planet’s upcoming climatic change.

Keywords

Climate crisis; global warming; recurrent neural networks; visualizations; climate change

9.1 Introduction

As illustrated in Fig. 9–1, the world’s present population of 8.1 billion is predicted to grow approximately 9.8 billion by 2050, corresponding to the U.S. Census Bureau—International Database (http://www.census.gov). This increase in population will raise demand for resources like food, materials, transportation, and energy, as well as raise the potential for deteriorating the environment.

Our planet has experienced drastic climatic changes over the past years. Scientists observed that global warming is now imminent owing to satellites orbiting the Earth and other innovations in technology. The mean ambient temperature of the world has grown by 1.62°F (0.9°C), since the late 19th century, mostly due to increased atmospheric emissions of CO2 and other substances caused by humans. The majority of the warming has happened in the last 35–40 years, which is entirely the result of human activities.

Arguably the biggest threat to civilization is impact of global warming, and its impacts are becoming ever more obvious: storms, droughts, fires, and flooding are becoming stronger and more common. Global environment is altering, affecting agricultural activities and natural resources that are essential to the survival of humanity. According to the 2018 global assessment of climate disruption, if greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are not eradicated globally within 30 years, catastrophic repercussions will befall the earth (David et al., 2022).

9.1.1 Global challenge

In addition to raising global temperatures, environmental change is also to blame for melting ice sheets, retreating glaciers, decreasing snowfall, rising sea levels, declining glaciers in the Arctic, and pH imbalances of oceans. Collectively, these problems create a global predicament.

[Imp Question] Will humanity be able to protect the Earth for coming generations?

Yes, the ability of mankind to mitigate global warming can be strengthened by computational intelligence.

9.1.2 Artificial intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) is described as the replication of cognitive abilities by machines, particularly automated systems. These procedures involve learning (the gathering of data and regulations to utilize it), conceiving (the application of principles to achieve tentative or precise outcomes), and self-rectification. AI is a wide phrase with two candidatures: machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).

9.1.3 Machine learning

With the use of ML, systems may turn automatically deft by collecting data, utilizing it to learn, and then creating computer programs that may utilize the knowledge gained to come up with conclusions.

9.1.4 Deep learning

DL arranges algorithms into layers to produce an artificial neural network (ANN) by its own; such a system is capable of acquiring information and rendering prudent decisions. ML has a subfield called DL. In the functioning of human brain, the term “deep” in DL implies to several layers of interactions or neurons.

AI has the potential to transform the entire field when implemented effectively. AI has the ability to bring about innovative advances in technology. The following are some potential applications of DL for Earth:

  • • Climatic modeling and weather forecasting
  • • Smart agriculture
  • • Distributed energy grids.

Public agencies (such as NASA) use this to improve the functionality and effectiveness of both climate and weather models. Sophisticated data, such as algorithms and scientific principles involving fluid dynamics in the oceans and atmosphere, are processed by these mathematical frameworks. The equations’ intricacy necessitates expensive, highly energy-intensive computation. Certain characteristics of these climatic simulations can be roughly matched by DL networks, which enables computing to operate significantly faster and include more variables from the real-world system when performing simulations. Such weather and climatic models can benefit from the use of AI approaches to address biases.

AI has tremendous potential for expediting the pursuit of remedies for climatic change. AI is assisting researchers and decision-makers in understanding and addressing the issue of climatic change: (1) collecting and evaluating information, (2) forecasting, (3) improving systems efficiency and predictive maintenance, and (4) facilitating the invention of next-generation technologies. Despite these promising developments, AI’s application in creating climatic solutions is still beset by three major obstacles.

Firstly, ML is being used on the other side of the balance.

  • • By 2025, the petroleum and natural gas sector is expected to make $400 billion in profits thanks to the deployment of AI to speed up exploration and production of gas and oil.
    Additionally, there’s the issue of AI’s green footprint, which is growing as its application and the need for processing power both expand.
  • • In 2019 the effect was quite minimal: AI contributed only a minor portion of the 1% to 2% worldwide information and communications technology sector’s GHG emissions. However, as AI is used more often and models get more sophisticated, its impact needs to be closely measured and monitored.
    The final difficulty is accuracy, especially when it comes to safety for people and infrastructures.
  • • Applying ML to power grid regulation and optimization, which has strict limitations. Repercussions of AI optimization might be a power outage, with associated financial losses and possibly even the forfeiture of life—things we definitely do not want—if the physics are not correct.
    Mitigation of climatic change is cutting emissions, while adaptation entails getting ready for inevitable outcomes.
  • • Modifications to land use, industry, buildings, transportation, and energy infrastructure are necessary to mitigate GHG emissions.
  • • Considering the climate and catastrophic occurrences, adaptation necessitates preparation for resilience and handling catastrophes.

ML has the potential to be a very effective instrument for lowering GHG emissions and assisting society in adapting to a changing environment. Both intriguing research questions and excellent commercial potential exist in smart grids to disaster management to identify high impact problems (the global effort against climate change) where ML can be used in conjunction with other disciplines to close current gaps.

A systematic review presented for hydrological processes climate change and earth systems using DL and ML (Ardabili et al., 2020). In an effort to improve urban resilience and reduce hazards to cities throughout the globe, a new viewpoint on the prediction of weather-related catastrophes has been offered. It relies on historic catastrophe data, computational models of the climate, and environmental measurements (Haggag et al., 2021). Chakrabortty et al. (2021) estimated flood susceptibility based on ANN, deep learning neural networks (DLNN), and data base (DB) algorithm approach. Wunsch et al. (2022) examined the direct effects that environmental change will have on Germany’s supplies of groundwater in the 21st century. The Earth surface is increasing its temperature according to the researchers at NASA, and the past two decades have seen several of the highest temperatures ever recorded (NASA, 2024). Lee et al. (2020) suggested a long-term, short-term memory framework, a data-based black-box technique, for the rainwater runoff monitoring procedure at the Kratie station on the main channel of the river Mekong. The initial DL-based forecasts of glacier formation were created by simulating the French Alps’ glacier evolution in the 21st century (Bolibar et al., 2022). Geographic engineering and the Earth’s surface temperature are the two fields of study that have made the greatest use of ML and DL algorithms in relation to mitigating and adapting to changing climates (Ladi et al., 2022). The LSTM beats the industry-standard exponential-smoothing and auto-regressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models by 32%–48% in synthesizing a prediction over five critical climate factors with an estimated overall root mean square error of 0.91 (Malik et al., 2023). Policymakers and other stakeholders should use these results as a reference when creating measures to reduce the impact of climate change on agricultural land and increase resilience. Using forecasting models and instances related to rising temperatures, a deep neural network projects potential environmental, economic, and risky situations related to hydrocarbons that are polycyclic aromatic in 2050 (Ki et al., 2021). According to the evaluation, in western and southern regions, cancer rates could rise by over 50%, surpassing the less-hazardous threshold. Lydiri et al. (2023) utilized a convolutional neural network to analyze Twitter users’ thoughts about the changing climate. The outcomes demonstrated that our method works better than the logistic regression, support vector machine, and naive Bayes ML techniques. In an area characterized by the southern monsoon, the effects of climate change as well as the high rainfall events that go along with it pose a serious danger to land resources (Paramita et al., 2022). To estimate the vulnerability of gully subsidence in the basin of River Dwarakeswar, researchers looked at ANN, SVM, and DLNN.

9.2 Deep learning models for climate change

In the global fight toward global warming, this chapter strives to give an extensive summary of the areas in which DL could prove very impactful when used through creative research or efficient engineering. One common DL technique for handling consecutive data is recurrent neural networks (RNNs). They have already been effectively used in a number of fields, including the processing of natural languages, language modeling, and voice recognition. Yet, the disappearing and ballooning gradient issues make retraining RNNs difficult. Many RNN architectures, such as gated recurrent unit (GRU) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have been put forward to address these problems. In this chapter, the authors compared these models and highlight their strengths and weaknesses.

9.2.1 Recurrent neural networks

Neural networks with loops that enable them to process sequential data are called RNNs. Unfortunately, the vanishing gradient problem impedes the conventional RNN’s ability to learn dependencies that persist. Two RNN variations that tackle this problem are GRU and LSTM. Sequential data processing and recurrence are the underlying principles of LSTMs, RNNs, and GRUs.

In an RNN, the result at each time step is dependent upon the preceding outputs as well as its input at that moment. An RNN with just one concealed layer and time-based backpropagation training resembles an Elman network, and it is the most basic type. Nevertheless, the issue of vanishing gradients impedes the typical RNN’s capacity to recognize dependencies that persist over time. Fig. 9–2 shows the representation of standard RNN and feed-forward network.

Fig. 9–3 displays the RNN unit’s architecture. It receives information from both present and prior steps. Here, tan  h serves as the activation function; however, you can also utilize different activation functions in its place. The primary characteristic of RNN is its utilization of layers that are concealed to solve problems. For the purpose of making predictions, RNNs can utilize concealed layers to aid in memory of the word (or data) sequence. The hidden state of RNN is given by

ht = tan  h(Whhht − 1+Wxhxt). (9–1)

(9–1)

9.2.2 Long short-term memory networks

LSTM was introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997). Periodically, an LSTM stores data within its memory cell. Three gates that are connected to the memory cell: the forget gate, the input gate, and the output gate. The input gate regulates how much fresh data are retained in a memory cell. The output gate regulates how much data are extracted out of the memory cell. The forget gate regulates how much data are erased from the memory cell. Essentially, each LSTM network has a trio of gates to regulate information flow and cells to store data as shown in Figs. 9–4 and 9–5. Data are carried by the cell states through the first step to all subsequent time steps without disappearing.

The following mathematical notations are used for the LSTM architecture:

ft = σg(Wfxt+Ufht − 1+bf)

it = σg(Wixt+Uiht − 1+bi)

Ot = σO(WOxt+UOht − 1+bO) (9–2)

(9–2)

Ct = ft ⊙ Ct − 1 + it ⊙ tan  h(Wcxt+Ucht − 1+bc)

ht = Ot ⊙ tan  h(Ct)

9.2.3 Gated recurrent unit networks

Cho et al. suggested GRU in 2014 (Cho et al., 2014). The flow of data is managed by GRU through the usage of gates as shown in Figs. 9–6 and 9–7. But there are just two gates on it: the reset gate and the update gate. The quantity of fresh data incorporated into the prior state is managed by the update gate. The quantity of prior data that is erased is managed by the reset gate. The GRU architecture employs the subsequent mathematical notations:

zt = σg(Wzxt+Uzht − 1+bz)

rt = σg(Wrxt+Urht − 1+br) (9–3)

(9–3)

ht = (1 − zt) ⊙ ht − 1 + zt ⊙ ϕh(Whxt+Uh(rt⊙ht − 1)+bh)

9.2.3.1 Long short-term memory versus gated recurrent unit

The employment of gates to regulate information flow is a common feature shared by GRU and LSTM. But GRU has just two gates, whereas LSTM has three. Because of this, LSTM is both more complicated and expressive than GRU. Additionally, LSTM and GRU differ in that the former contains a distinct memory cell while the latter merges them into one vector of memory. The effectiveness of LSTM as well as GRU across a variety of tasks (including sentiment analysis, language modeling, and speech recognition) has been examined in a number of studies. The findings are conflicting; whereas some research indicate that LSTM works better than GRU, others suggest the contrary. The majority of research, however, concur that both LSTM as well GRU are equally useful when analyzing sequential data, although the particular job and dataset will determine how well each model performs.

9.2.4 Mathematical equations for MSE, MAE, MAPE, and R2

To assess the accuracy of the network, mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and R-squared (R2) are calculated by Eqs. (9–4), (9–5), (9–6), and (9–7), respectively.

${MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( {y_{actual} - y_{predicted}} \right)^{2}$ (9–4)

(9–4)

${MAE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left| {y_{actual} - y_{predicted}} \right|$ (9–5)

(9–5)

${MAPE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left| \frac{y_{actual} - y_{predicted}}{y_{actual}} \right|$ (9–6)

(9–6)

$R^{2} = 1 - \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( {y_{actual} - y_{predicted}} \right)^{2}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{N}\left( {y_{mean} - y_{actual}} \right)^{2}},$ (9–7)

(9–7)

where ypredicted represents the output of the ANN model, yactual is the results of the numerical simulation, N is the total amount of data, and ymean is the mean of the numerical simulation results for all data points.

9.2.5 Mathematical equations for optimizers: Adam, SGD, Adamax, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSProp, and Nadam

In this chapter, the following equations are used to better understand the properties of optimizers:

9.2.5.1 Adagrad

$\theta_{t + 1} = \theta_{t} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{G_{t} + \epsilon}}g_{t},$ (9–8)

(9–8)

where θt is the node weight for generation t, η is the learning rate, gt is the vector of gradients for the current generation, Gt is a diagonal matrix containing the squares of all previous gradients, and ϵ is a very small term that provides numerical stability.

9.2.5.2 Adamax

$\left. \begin{matrix} {m_{t} = \beta_{1}m_{t - 1} + \left( {1 - \beta_{1}} \right)g_{t}} \\ \quad \\ {v_{t} = \beta_{1}v_{t - 1} + \left( {1 - \beta_{2}} \right){g_{t}}^{2}} \\ \end{matrix} \right\},$ (9–9)

(9–9)

where mt is an exponentially decaying average of past gradients, β1(=0.900 in Keras) is the decay rate, vt is an exponentially decaying average of past squared gradients, and β2(=0.999 in Keras) is the decay rate.

9.2.5.3 Adam

vt = max (β2vt − 1,|gt|) (9–10)

(9–10)

9.2.5.4 SGD

The following equation is used to generate a new sequence of data with less noise:

vt = βvt − 1 + (1−β)st,

where st is the noisy data generated in time t.

The following equations are used to update weights (w) and bias (b) in SGD:

$\left. \begin{matrix} {w_{t} = w_{t - 1} - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{t - 1}}} \\ \quad \\ {b_{t} = b_{t - 1} - \eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_{t - 1}}} \\ \end{matrix} \right\},$ (9–11)

(9–11)

where $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$ is the derivative of loss with respect to weight and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$ is the derivative of loss with respect to bias.

9.2.5.5 Adadelta

$w_{t} = w_{t - 1} - \eta_{t}^{\prime}\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{t - 1}}{with}\eta_{t}^{\prime} = \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{g_{t} + \varepsilon}},$ (9–12)

(9–12)

where

$g_{t} = \beta g_{t - 1} + \left( {1 - \beta} \right)\left\lbrack \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{t - 1}} \right\rbrack^{2}.$ (9–13)

(9–13)

9.2.5.6 RMSProp

$\left. \begin{matrix} {w_{t} = w_{t - 1} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{E\left\lbrack g^{2} \right\rbrack}}\frac{\partial c}{\partial w_{t - 1}}} \\ \quad \\ {{E\left\lbrack g^{2} \right\rbrack}_{t} = \beta{E\left\lbrack g^{2} \right\rbrack}_{t - 1} + \left( {1 - \beta} \right)\left\lbrack \frac{\partial c}{\partial w_{t - 1}} \right\rbrack^{2}} \\ \end{matrix} \right\},$ (9–14)

(9–14)

where E[g] is the moving average of squared gradients, and $\frac{\partial c}{\partial w}$ is the gradient of the cost function with respect to the weight.

9.2.5.7 Nadam

$\theta_{t + 1} = \theta_{t} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{{\widehat{v}}_{t}} + \epsilon}\left( {\beta_{1}{\widehat{m}}_{t} + \frac{1 - \beta_{1}}{1 - \beta_{1}^{t}}g}_{t} \right),$ (9–15)

(9–15)

where ${\widehat{m}}_{t} = \frac{m_{t}}{1 - \beta_{1}^{t}}$ and ${\widehat{v}}_{t} = \frac{v_{t}}{1 - \beta_{2}^{t}}$.

9.3 Operations in python framework using Jupyter Notebook

In this chapter, the raw dirty global datasets are collected from Berkeley Earth (http://berkeleyearth.org/data/). It offers gridded data on temperatures as well as superior resolution time series data for both land and sea from 1750. The following newest generation of products are augmented by ML techniques to improve the spatial resolution:

  • • GlobalLandTemperaturesByCountry.csv (Country-wise Global Average Land Temperature)
  • • GlobalLandTemperaturesByState.csv (State-wise Global Average Land Temperature)
  • • GlobalLandTemperaturesByMajorCity.csv (Global Land Temperatures by major city)
  • • GlobalLandTemperaturesByCity.csv (City-wise Global Land Temperature)
  • • GlobalTemperatures.csv (Global Temperatures of Land and Ocean-and-Land).

The raw dirty dataset which requires lots of data cleaning and preprocessing. After performing necessary feature engineering steps and exploring the data with visualizations, data are prepared to feed into the models. After that, the models are built, trained, and evaluated for tasks: predicting global temperature trend and predicting US and India temperature trend. The following operations are performed for the trends:

9.4 Exploring visualizations for climate models

Figs. 9–8 and 9–9 show the country-wise count of average temperature and country-wise uncertainty count of average temperature, respectively. The average global land temperatures ranging from −20°C to 30°C as shown in Fig. 9–10. Figs. 9–11 to 9–15 show the global temperature change in 1743, 1800, 1900, 2000 and 2013, respectively. The average land temperatures globally as shown in Fig. 9–16, and it is observed that the variation of temperature ranging from 15°C to 19°C before 1860. But due to the climate change globally, the variation of temperature was observed, ranging from 19°C to 21°C, in 2013. Fig. 9–17 shows the US temperature data from 1800 to 2013, which varies from −10°C to 25°C, and the India temperature data from 1800 to 2013 is plotted as shown in Fig. 9–18, which varies from 5°C to 35°C due to the climate change. Fig. 9–19 shows the history of training set and testing set, and the year-wise actual and prediction values of temperature is shown in Fig. 9–20. The error in actual and prediction values of temperature is shown in Fig. 9–21, and the error in temperature is plotted as shown in Fig. 9–22.

To produce predictions or judgements, a model is trained using a dataset within both ML and DL systems. The process of optimization, which entails determining the ideal model parameter set to minimize errors or losses on the data being trained, is a crucial step in the training process. The optimization algorithm is essential to the success of any DL program. Algorithms called optimizers are employed in the training phase in order to determine the ideal model’s parameter configuration. The aforementioned techniques iteratively modify the model’s weights and prejudices until they reach an optimal loss value.

Numerous optimizers are available from Keras for neural network model training. The following optimization algorithm are used in the present DL in order to enhance the training of neural networks:

  • • Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)
  • • Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
  • • Adaptive Moment Estimation with Infinity Norm (Adamax)
  • • Adaptive Gradient Algorithm (Adagrad)
  • • Adaptive Delta (Adadelta)
  • • Root Mean Square Propagation (RMSProp)
  • • Nesterov Adaptive Moment Estimation (Nadam).

In the first step, LSTM model is built and trained for predicting global temperature trend with activation=linear, optimizer=adam, and loss=mse. In the second step, GRU model is built and trained for predicting global temperature trend with activation=linear, optimizer=adam, and loss=mse. In the third step, RNN model is built and trained for predicting global temperature trend with activation=linear, optimizer=adam, and loss=mse. 9.5 Conclusions and recommendations

This chapter describes a methodology for the modeling of climate change in terms of global temperature using DL models within python framework. Raw and dirty global datasets are collected from Berkeley Earth (http://berkeleyearth.org/data/). It offers data on temperatures in grid format together with superior resolution time series data for both land and sea from 1743 to 2013. Three popular neural networks such as RNN, LSTM, and GRU are built, trained, and evaluated using various optimizers like Adam, SGD, Adamax, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop, and Nadam for predicting global temperature trend as well as predicting US and India temperature trend. The main contributions of the present chapter are as follows:

  1. 1. With Adam optimizer, faster training and computationally less expensive possible using LSTM, followed by GRU and RNN. The mean square errors are: MSE=0.09250031065887551 (LSTM), MSE=0.08040434597627735 (GRU), MSE=0.06096303859943463 (RNN)
  2. 2. Using SGD optimizer, LSTM prediction is good, followed by GRU and RNN. The mean square errors are: MSE=1.8776324756386953 (LSTM), MSE=0.9815534033191056 (GRU), MSE=0.11220742113813277 (RNN)
  3. 3. With Adamax optimizer, LSTM prediction is good, followed by RNN and GRU. The mean square errors are: MSE=0.0998461682132788 (LSTM), MSE=0.09855693036455689 (RNN), MSE=0.09817570471281879 (GRU)
  4. 4. Using Adagrad and Adadelta optimizers, LSTM prediction is good, followed by GRU and RNN. The mean square errors are: MSE=22.645661292549917 (LSTM with Adagrad), MSE=2.210322750347732 (GRU with Adagrad), MSE=0.22145172804570754 (RNN with Adagrad), MSE=49.68461904083209 (LSTM with Adadelta), MSE=41.480035564039305 (GRU with Adadelta), MSE=13.816304188418261 (RNN with Adadelta)
  5. 5. With RMSProp optimizer, GRU prediction is good, followed by RNN and LSTM. The mean square errors are: MSE=0.10032250216117587 (GRU), MSE=0.08745906210421796 (RNN), MSE=0.07977269791361769 (LSTM)
  6. 6. LSTM prediction is good, followed by RNN and GRU using Nadam optimizer. The mean square errors are: MSE=0.09401263234931696 (LSTM), MSE=0.0772197251373337 (RNN), MSE=0.07443513244167563 (GRU).

The DL models illustrated in the present chapter could be utilized to forecast the planet’s upcoming climatic change.
